name: Dot-Com Bubble Parallel
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Pets.com and the Quantum Hype Cycle
lesson.summary: The dot-com crash did not prove the internet was fake, it proved that a real technology and an irrational market for that technology are separate questions, a distinction the current quantum computing boom needs badly.
lesson.body:
Technology bubbles have a recognizable shape: a genuinely useful innovation appears, capital floods toward anything associated with it, valuations detach from any plausible revenue path, and then a correction forces a re-pricing based on which companies and use cases actually work. The dot-com bubble of the late 1990s is the clearest modern case study, and it is worth examining closely before applying its lessons to quantum computing, because the lesson people usually draw from it is wrong.

The NASDAQ composite index rose from roughly 1,000 points in the mid-1990s to around 5,000 by March 2000, driven substantially by internet-related stocks that had little or no earnings. Over the following two and a half years the index fell by roughly three quarters. Household names like Pets.com and Webvan, both well funded and widely covered by the press, burned through their capital and shut down. Even Amazon, which survived and eventually became one of the most valuable companies in the world, saw its stock price fall by more than ninety percent from its peak and came close to running short on cash.

Here is the part that gets lost in retellings: the internet was not a mirage. It went on to reorganize retail, media, communication, logistics, and advertising, arguably qualifying as one of the most consequential general purpose technologies of the last century. The bubble was not a referendum on whether the internet mattered. It was a referendum on which specific companies, business models, and timelines were viable in 1999, and on that question the market was mostly wrong in the short run and roughly right in the long run.

This produces two symmetrical errors that are equally unhelpful. The first is bubble denial after the fact: because the crash happened, some people concluded the internet itself had been oversold and would fade, a claim that aged badly within a decade. The second is retroactive vindication: because the internet turned out to be transformative, some people now argue that 1999-era valuations were basically fine and the crash was just noise, which ignores that thousands of companies and enormous sums of capital were genuinely destroyed on bad bets.

Quantum computing enthusiasm today shares the structural features of a bubble: rapid capital inflows, richly valued pre-revenue and early-revenue companies, and press coverage that treats every incremental hardware milestone as a breakthrough. That resemblance tells us something about market psychology, but on its own it tells us nothing about whether quantum computing is more like the internet, a real general purpose technology whose short-term pricing simply got ahead of itself, or something narrower whose long-run payoff never arrives at anything close to current expectations. Answering that requires judging quantum computing on its own technical merits, which is exactly what the general purpose technology tests in the next chapters are built to do.
